props.title: Into the Mirror

sections.content: Into the Mirror (2003) launched a wave of innovative Korean horror films exploring reflections, doppelgangers, and retail spaces as sites of supernatural terror. Director Kim Sung-ho crafts a mesmerizing psychological thriller that would later inspire Alexandre Aja's Mirrors (2008), though the original remains superior in its subtle exploration of identity and corporate malaise. Like A Tale of Two Sisters (2003) from the same year, it demonstrates Korean cinema's masterful blend of atmospheric horror with deep psychological undertones.

sections.content: The film's department store setting taps into a rich vein of retail horror that includes Dawn of the Dead (1978) and Phantom of the Mall: Eric's Revenge (1989). These commercial spaces become uncanny domains where capitalism and consumerism twist into something sinister. Into the Mirror particularly excels in using reflective surfaces - windows, mirrors, chrome fixtures - to create a constant sense of unease and displacement.

The influence of Into the Mirror can be seen in later Asian horror films dealing with reflections and doubles, like The Eye (2002) and Dark Water (2002). Its innovative use of mirror imagery and practical effects over CGI created a template for supernatural horror that prioritizes psychological dread over jump scares. movies.title: Dark Water
movies.slug: A mother and daughter move into an apartment with mysterious water leaks and reflective surfaces hiding dark secrets

sections.content: While Into the Mirror draws from earlier mirror-focused horror like Candyman (1992), it revolutionized the subgenre through its incorporation of Buddhist concepts about reflection and reality. This spiritual dimension adds layers of meaning absent from more straightforward evil mirror films like Mirror Mirror (1990) or Urban Legend (1998).
